They say: "al-qab" is half a finger's length. Some of them said: it was the span of two cubits between them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the report of Ibn Wahb. And in the hadith of al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from Jabir, there is a witness to this.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Talq ibn Ghannam, from Za'idah, from al-Shaybani, who said: I asked Zirr about the statement: ﴿Then he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. He said: 'Abdullah told us that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bazi' al-Baghdadi narrated to me, Ishaq ibn Mansur narrated to us, Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, from 'Abdullah regarding: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril in two garments of green silk (rafraf), which filled what was between the heaven and the earth.

Based on what we have mentioned, His statement ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ means: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad, what he revealed. Or: Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad what He revealed through Jibril. Both meanings are correct. It has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His statement ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ that he said: He revealed to him: "Did We not find you an orphan?" ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharh: 4].

Others said: Allah revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it.

* *

As for His statement ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw. Will you then dispute with him over what he saw?﴾, Muslim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from Ziyad ibn Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ and ﴿He saw him in another descent﴾, he said: He saw him with his heart twice.

Similarly, Simak narrated it from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it. Likewise Abu Salih, al-Suddi and others said: He saw him with his heart twice [or once]. It has been opposed by Ibn Mas'ud and others. In one report from him (Ibn 'Abbas) he stated the seeing without qualification, and it is to be understood as restricted to the heart. As for whoever narrated from him that it was with the eye, he is unusual, for nothing authentic has come on this from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The statement of al-Baghawi in his tafsir: "A group went to the view that he saw Him with his own eye, and this is the view of Anas, al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah" — it is open to scrutiny, and Allah knows best.

Al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Nabhan ibn Safwan narrated to us, Yahya ibn Kathir al-'Anbari narrated to us, from Salm ibn Ja'far, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Muhammad saw his Lord. I said: Does not Allah say: ﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives all vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103]? He said: Woe to you! That is when He manifests Himself with His light which is His light; and he saw his Lord twice.

Then he said: Hasan gharib.

He also said: Ibn Abi 'Umar narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi who said: Ibn 'Abbas met Ka'b at 'Arafah, and asked him about something, and he exclaimed "Allahu akbar" until the mountains echoed back to him. Ibn 'Abbas said: We are the Banu Hashim. Ka'b said: Allah divided His seeing and His speech between Muhammad and Musa: Musa spoke with Him twice, and Muhammad saw Him twice. Masruq said: I entered upon 'Aishah and said: Did Muhammad see his Lord? She said: You have said something at which my hair stood on end. I said: Gently, then I recited: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾.

She said: Where are you being taken? It was only Jibril. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord, or that he concealed something of what he was commanded, or that he knows the five things which Allah, the Exalted, mentioned: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman: 34] — he has indeed uttered a great slander. Rather, he saw Jibril in his form only twice: once at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Jiyad, and he had six hundred wings, having filled the horizon.

Al-Nasa'i said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Do you wonder that the garment belongs to Ibrahim, the speech to Musa, and the seeing to Muhammad, peace be upon them?!

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "There is light; how could I see Him?" In another narration: "I saw a light."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Abu Khalid narrated to us, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart twice." Then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Ibn Humayd, from Mihran, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I did not see Him with my eye, but I saw Him with my heart twice," then he recited: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari narrated to us, 'Abbad ibn Mansur informed me who said: I asked 'Ikrimah: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. 'Ikrimah said: Do you want me to tell you that he has seen Him? I said: Yes. He said: He has seen Him, and then he has seen Him. He said: I asked al-Hasan about it, and he said: He saw His majesty, His greatness, and His robe.

And my father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Mujahid narrated to us, Abu 'Amir al-'Aqadi narrated to us, Abu Khaldah informed us, from Abu al-'Aliyah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and I saw behind the river a veil, and I saw behind the veil a light, I did not see other than that." [Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it as in al-Durr al-Manthur, and it is mursal.]

That is very unusual. As for the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad:

Aswad ibn 'Amir narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord, Mighty and Majestic."

Its chain is according to the conditions of the sahih, but it is an abridgement of the hadith of the dream, as Imam Ahmad also narrated:

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My Lord came to me last night in the best of forms — I think he meant in sleep — and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know over what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?'" He said: "I said: No. So He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coldness between my breasts — or he said my chest — and I knew what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. Then He said: 'O Muhammad, do you know over what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?'" He said: "I said: Yes, they dispute over the expiations and the degrees." He said: "And what are the expiations and the degrees?" He said: "I said: Remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, and completing ablution in hardship. Whoever does this lives in goodness, dies in goodness, and is free from his sins like the day his mother bore him. And He said: 'Say, O Muhammad, when you pray: O Allah, I ask You for good deeds and to abandon evil deeds, and love for the poor. And if You intend a trial for Your servants, take me to You without being tried.'" He said: "And the degrees are giving food, spreading the greeting of peace, and praying at night while people sleep."

It has already been mentioned at the end of Surah Sad, from Mu'adh, something similar. Ibn Jarir narrated it by another route from Ibn 'Abbas, and in it there is a different context and a strange addition, so he said:

Ahmad ibn 'Isa al-Tamimi narrated to me, Sulayman ibn 'Umar ibn Sayyar narrated to me, my father narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Zarbi, from Umar ibn Sulayman, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord in the best of forms, and He said to me: 'O Muhammad, do you know over what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?' I said: 'No, my Lord.' So He placed His hand between my shoulders, and I found its coldness between my breasts, and I knew what is in the heavens and the earth. I said: 'O my Lord, over the degrees and the expiations, and transferring the feet to the congregations, and waiting for prayer after prayer.' I said: 'O my Lord, You took Ibrahim as a friend and You spoke to Musa directly, and You did such and such.' He said: 'Did I not expand your breast? Did I not remove from you your burden? Did I not do for you? Did I not do?'" He said: "Then He conveyed to me things which I was not permitted to tell you." He said: "That is His statement in His Book: ﴿Then he drew near and descended. And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed. The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾; so He placed the light of my sight in my heart, and I looked at Him with my heart." Its chain is weak.

Al-Hafiz Ibn 'Asakir mentioned with his chain to Habbar ibn al-Aswad, may Allah be pleased with him, that 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, when he went out on a trade journey to Syria, said to the people of Makkah: "Know that I disbelieve in the One who drew near and descended." The statement reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Allah has set upon him one of His dogs." Habbar said: I was with them, and we alighted in a land abounding in lions. He said: I saw the lion come and begin to sniff the heads of the people one by one, until it reached 'Utbah and seized his head from among them.

Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned in the Sirah that this was in the land of al-Zarqa', and it was said: in al-Sarah; and that he feared that night, and they placed him among them and slept around him; the lion came and began to roar, then it stepped over them to him and crushed his head — may Allah curse him.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge﴾. This was the second time the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril in his true form in which God created him, and it was on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). We have already presented the hadiths about the Isra', with their chains and wordings, at the beginning of the chapter "Subhan" (Surah al-Isra'), so there is no need to repeat them here. It has been mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, affirmed that the Prophet saw his Lord on the night of the Isra', and he cited this verse as evidence. A group of the early and later scholars followed him, while groups of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, the Successors and others disagreed with him.

Imam Ahmad said: Hasan ibn Musa narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud concerning this verse, ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril, and he had six hundred wings, and from his feathers were scattered the tahawil (pearls and rubies)." [[Musnad (1/460).]] This is a good and strong chain (isnad: the chain of narrators).

Ahmad also said: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, Sharik narrated to us, from Jami' ibn Abi Rashid, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril in his form, and he had six hundred wings, each wing of which had blocked the horizon. From his wing there would fall tahawil, pearls and rubies, which only God knows. [[I did not find it in the Musnad, but al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned it in Atraf al-Musnad (4/158).]] Its chain is also good.

Ahmad also said: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Husayn narrated to me, 'Asim ibn Bahdalah narrated to me, who said: I heard Shaqiq ibn Salamah saying: I heard Ibn Mas'ud saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he had six hundred wings." I asked 'Asim about the wings, but he refused to tell me. Then one of his companions informed me that the wing is what lies between the east and the west. [[Musnad (1/407).]] This is also a good chain.

Ahmad said: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Husayn narrated to us, 'Asim ibn Bahdalah narrated to me, [[In A: "Husayn."]] Shaqiq narrated to me, [[In M: "Shaqiq ibn Salamah."]] who said: [[In M, A: "He said."]] I heard Ibn Mas'ud saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me wearing a green garment on which there were pearls." [[Musnad (1/407).]] Its chain is also good.

Imam Ahmad said: Yahya narrated to me, from Isma'il, Amir narrated to us, who said: Masruq came to 'A'ishah and said: O Mother of the Believers, did Muhammad (ﷺ) see his Lord, Mighty and Majestic? She said: Glory be to God! My hair stood on end at what you have said. Where are you from three things? Whoever tells you any of them has lied. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord has lied. Then she recited: ﴿No vision perceives Him, but He perceives all vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103], and ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. Whoever tells you that he knows what will happen tomorrow has lied. Then she recited: ﴿Indeed, God has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs﴾ [Luqman: 34] to the end of the verse. Whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed something has lied. Then she recited: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. Rather, he saw Jibril in his form twice. [[Musnad (6/49).]]

Ahmad also said: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, who said: I was with 'A'ishah and I said: Does not God say: ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir: 23], and ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾? She said: I am the first of this Ummah to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "That was only Jibril. I have not seen him in his form in which he was created except twice: I saw him descending from the sky to the earth, filling the vastness of his creation between the sky and the earth."

Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in their Sahihs, through the hadith of al-Sha'bi with this chain. [[Musnad (6/241), Sahih al-Bukhari no. (4855), and Sahih Muslim no. (177), in similar wording.]]

The narration of Abu Dharr: Imam Ahmad said: 'Affan narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, Qatadah narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, who said: I said to Abu Dharr: If I had seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would have asked him. He said: What would you have asked him? He said: I would have asked him: Did he see his Lord, Mighty and Majestic? He said: I did ask him, and he said: "I saw Him as light; how could I see Him?" [[Musnad (5/147).]]

This is what occurs in the narration of Imam Ahmad. Muslim also recorded it through two routes with two wordings. He said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, from Qatadah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Did you see your Lord? He said: "Light; how could I see Him?"

And he said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, my father narrated to us, from Qatadah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, who said: I said to Abu Dharr: If I had seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would have asked him. He said: About what would you have asked him? I said: I would have asked him: Did you see your Lord? Abu Dharr said: I did ask, and he said: "I saw light." [[Sahih Muslim no. (178).]]

Al-Khallal in his book "al-'Ilal" related that Imam Ahmad was asked about this hadith and said: I have always disapproved of it, and I do not know its meaning. [[The objection has no basis in the text, for it has supporting narrations, and it is evidence for the negation of seeing God in this world.]]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, 'Amr ibn 'Awn al-Wasiti narrated to us, Hushaym informed us, from Mansur, from al-Hakam, from Ibrahim, from his father, from Abu Dharr, who said: He saw Him with his heart, and did not see Him with his eye.

Ibn Khuzaymah tried to claim that there is a break in the chain between 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq and Abu Dharr. As for Ibn al-Jawzi, he interpreted it to mean that Abu Dharr perhaps asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before the Isra', and he answered him with what he answered; and if he had asked him after the Isra', he would have answered with affirmation. But this is very weak, for 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, may God be pleased with her, asked about it after the Isra', and it was not affirmed for her. Whoever says that he addressed her according to the level of her understanding, or tried to show her to be mistaken in what she held, such as Ibn Khuzaymah in his book "al-Tawhid" [[al-Tawhid of Ibn Khuzaymah (pp. 205, 206) (p. 225).]], then he himself is the one in error. And God knows best.

Al-Nasa'i said: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Hisham narrated to us, from Mansur, from al-Hakam, from Yazid ibn Shurayk, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, saw his Lord with his heart, and did not see Him with his eyes. [[al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra no. (11536).]]

It is established in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, from 'Ali ibn Mushir, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that he said concerning the verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾: He saw Jibril, peace be upon him. [[In A: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril."]] [[Sahih Muslim no. (175).]]

Mujahid said concerning the verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾: He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril in his form twice. Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said the same.

* *

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾: It has already been mentioned in the hadiths of the Isra' that the angels covered it like crows, and the light of the Lord covered it, and colours covered it, which I do not know what they are.

Imam Ahmad said: Malik ibn Mighwal narrated to us, al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi narrated to us, from Talhah, from Murrah, from 'Abd Allah, that is Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, which is in the seventh heaven, to which whatever ascends from the earth ends, and it is taken from there; and to which whatever descends from above it ends, and it is taken from there. ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾. He said: It was a carpet of gold. He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever of his Ummah does not associate anything with God will be forgiven the grave sins. Muslim alone narrated it. [[Musnad (1/422) and Sahih Muslim no. (173).]]

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or another (Abu Ja'far was in doubt), who said: When the Messenger of God was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree, and it was said to him: This is the Lote-tree. [He said:] And the light of the Creator covered it, and the angels covered it like crows when they alight on a tree. He said: Then He spoke to him at that moment, and said to him: Ask.

Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid: ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾: He said: The branches of the Lote-tree were pearls, rubies and emeralds, and Muhammad saw it, and saw his Lord with his heart.

Ibn Zayd said: It was said: O Messenger of God, what did you see covering that Lote-tree? He said: "I saw a carpet of gold covering it, and I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying God, Mighty and Majestic." [[This is one of the mursal reports (lacking a Companion in the chain) of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who is weak.]]

* *

His saying: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It did not turn right or left. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: it did not go beyond what he was commanded.

This is a great attribute of steadfastness and obedience, for he did only what he was commanded, and he did not ask for more than he was given. How excellent is what the poet (al-Nazim) said:

He saw the Garden of Refuge and what lies above it, and had another seen what he saw, he would have been bewildered.

* *

His saying: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, like His saying: ﴿That We may show you of Our signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23], meaning: which indicate Our power and Our greatness. By these two verses, those among the People of the Sunnah who hold that the seeing (of God) did not occur that night have derived evidence; for He said: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, and if he had seen his Lord, he would have reported that and said so to the people. This has already been established in Surat al-Isra'. Imam Ahmad said:

Abu al-Nadr narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Talhah narrated to us, from al-Walid ibn Qays, from Ishaq ibn Abi al-Kahtalah. Muhammad said: I think it is from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: Muhammad did not see Jibril in his form except twice. As for one time, he asked him to show him himself in his form, and he showed him his form, and it filled the horizon. As for the other, he ascended with him when he ascended. And His saying: ﴿while he was at the highest horizon. Then he approached and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. And He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. He said: When Jibril perceived his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, he returned to his form and prostrated. So His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge, when there covered the Lote-tree that which covered. His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress. He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾: he said: [it refers to] the creation of Jibril, peace be upon him.

This is how Imam Ahmad narrated it, and it is strange (gharib). [[Musnad (1/407).]]

Ibn Kathir's commentary on Surah al-Najm (53), verses 5–18 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, exalted is He, says, informing about His servant and messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), that the one who taught him, the one who brought it to mankind, is ﴿mighty in power﴾. This is Gabriel (peace be upon him), as He said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, obeyed and trustworthy﴾ [At-Takwir: 19–21].

Here He says ﴿dhu mirrah﴾, meaning possessor of strength. This was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Abbas said: possessor of a fine appearance.

Qatadah said: possessor of a tall and handsome form.

There is no contradiction between the two statements, for he (peace be upon him) had a fine appearance and great strength. In the authentic hadith narrated through Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Amr, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity is not lawful for the rich, nor for one who possesses mirrah and is sound [of body]." [[The hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr is narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan, no. 1634, and by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan, no. 652, from Rayhan ibn Yazid, from him. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is narrated by al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (5/99) and Ibn Majah in his Sunan, no. 1839, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from him.]]

* *

His words ﴿Then he stood﴾ refer to Gabriel (peace be upon him). This was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

﴿while he was at the higher horizon﴾ refers to Gabriel, who stood at the higher horizon. This was said by 'Ikrimah and others. 'Ikrimah said: The higher horizon is the one from which the dawn comes. Mujahid said: it is the place where the sun rises. Qatadah said: it is the one from which the daytime comes. Ibn Zayd and others said likewise.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Zur'ah narrated to us, Musarrif ibn 'Amr al-Yami Abu al-Qasim narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Talhah ibn Musarrif narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from al-Walid (that is, Ibn Qays), from Ishaq ibn Abi al-Kahtalah, I think he mentioned it from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not see Gabriel in his [true] form except twice. The first time, he asked him to show himself in his form, and he filled the horizon. The second time, he was with him when he ascended, and that is His words: ﴿while he was at the higher horizon﴾.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) has made a statement here that I have not seen from anyone else, nor has he attributed it to anyone. Its essence is that he took the meaning to be: ﴿Then he stood﴾, that is, this mighty one of power, possessor of strength, together with Muhammad (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon both of them), ﴿while he was at the higher horizon﴾, that is, both of them stood together at the horizon, and that was on the night of the Isra'. Thus he said, and no one agreed with him in this. Then he proceeded to justify what he said from the standpoint of Arabic grammar (al-'Arabiyyah), and said: This is like His words: ﴿When we are dust and our fathers [are brought forth]?﴾ [An-Naml: 67], where he joined "al-aba'" (the fathers) to the pronoun in "kunna" (we were) without making "nahnu" (we) explicit. Likewise His words: ﴿Then he stood, while he﴾. He said: al-Farra' mentioned from some of the Arabs that he recited:

Have you not seen that the nab' tree hardens its wood,
while the brittle castor plant does not stand alike?

[The line is in Tafsir al-Tabari (27/25) and is by Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah.]

What he said from the standpoint of Arabic grammar is sound, but the meaning does not support it, for this vision of Gabriel was not on the night of the Isra'; rather it was before that, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on the earth. Gabriel descended to him and drew near to him, while he was in the form in which Allah created him, having six hundred wings. Then he saw him another time, a descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), that is, on the night of the Isra'. This first vision was in the early days of the prophethood, after Gabriel (peace be upon him) had come to him for the first time, when Allah revealed to him the opening verses of "Iqra'" (Surah al-'Alaq). Then the revelation paused for a period, during which the Prophet (ﷺ) went out many times, intending to throw himself from the mountain peaks. Whenever he was about to do that, Gabriel would call out to him from the air: "O Muhammad, you are truly the Messenger of Allah, and I am Gabriel." Thereby his heart would be calmed and his eye comforted. Whenever the matter lasted long for him, he would return to it again, until Gabriel appeared to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in al-Abtah, in his form in which Allah created him, having six hundred wings, which filled the horizon with the greatness of his body. He drew near to him and revealed to him from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, what He commanded him. At that moment he recognized the greatness of the angel who had brought him the message, the nobility of his rank, and the high station he held with his Creator who had sent him.

As for the hadith which the memorizer (al-Hafiz) Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated in his Musnad, where he said:

Salamah ibn Shabib narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated to us, al-Harith ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us, from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While I was sitting, Gabriel (peace be upon him) came, and struck between my shoulders. I rose toward a tree in which there were two nests of birds, and he sat in one of them and I sat in the other. It rose and ascended until it filled the two horizons, while I was turning my gaze. Had I wished to touch the sky, I would have touched it. Gabriel turned to me as if he were a rug laid down, and I recognized the excellence of his knowledge of Allah over me. A door of the doors of heaven was opened for me, and I saw the Greatest Light, and beneath the Veil was a fluttering of pearls and rubies. And what Allah willed to reveal was revealed to me."

Then al-Bazzar said: No one narrates it except al-Harith ibn 'Ubayd, and he was a well-known man from the people of Basra. [[Musnad al-Bazzar, no. 58.]]

I say: This al-Harith ibn 'Ubayd is Abu Qudamah al-Iyadi. Muslim included him in his Sahih, but Ibn Ma'in weakened him and said: he is not anything. Imam Ahmad said: his hadith is inconsistent (mudtarib). Abu Hatim al-Razi said: his hadith is written down but is not used as evidence. Ibn Hibban said: his errors are many, so it is not permissible to use him as evidence when he is alone in a narration. This hadith is among his strange narrations, for it contains strangeness, unusual wording, and a strange context. Perhaps it was a dream, and Allah knows best.

Imam Ahmad said: Hajjaj narrated to us, Shurayk narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Gabriel in his form, and he had six hundred wings, each wing of which filled the horizon. From his wings there fell pearls, rubies and colored decorations, which only Allah knows. Ahmad alone narrated it. [[Al-Musnad (1/395).]]

Ahmad also said: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from Idris ibn Munabbih, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) asked Gabriel to show himself to him in his form. He said: "Ask your Lord." So he asked his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and a dark mass appeared to him from the east, which rose and spread out. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw it, he fainted. Gabriel came to him, supported him, and wiped the foam from his mouth.

Ahmad alone narrated it. [[Al-Musnad (1/322).]] Ibn 'Asakir also narrated it in the biography of 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, through the route of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from Habbar ibn al-Aswad, who said: Abu Lahab and his son 'Utbah had prepared to go to Syria, and I prepared with them. His son 'Utbah said: "By Allah, I will go to Muhammad and I will harm him concerning his Lord, Glorified is He." So he went until he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, he (Allah) disbelieves in the One who drew near and came down, so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, send against him one of Your dogs." Then he left him and returned to his father. His father said: "My son, what did you say to him?" He told him what he had said to him. He said: "What did he say to you?" He said: "He said: 'O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs.'" He said: "My son, by Allah, I do not feel safe from his supplication against you." So we travelled until we stopped at al-Shurah, which was a lion-infested place, and we went down to the hermitage of a monk. The monk said: "O company of the Arabs, what brought you to this land? Lions roam in it as sheep roam." Abu Lahab said to us: "You know my old age and my right, and this man has made a supplication against my son, which, by Allah, I do not feel safe from. So gather your goods at this hermitage, spread them out for my son upon it, then spread out around it." We did so, and the lion came and smelled our faces. When it did not find what it wanted, it crouched, then leapt, and behold, it was on top of the goods. It smelled his face, then struck him a blow that crushed his head. Abu Lahab said: "I knew that he would not escape the supplication of Muhammad." [[I have not found the biography of 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab in the manuscript of Tarikh Dimashq, nor in its abridgment by Ibn Manzur.]]

* *

His words ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾ mean: Gabriel drew near to Muhammad when he descended to him on the earth, until there was between him and Muhammad (ﷺ) the distance of two bow-lengths, that is, the measure of the two when they are stretched. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

It has also been said that what is meant is the distance between the string of the bow and its belly (the wooden body).

* *

His words ﴿or nearer﴾: it has already been mentioned that this expression is used in the language to affirm what is being reported and to negate anything beyond it, as in His words: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74], meaning: they are not softer than stones, rather they are like them or exceed them in hardness and severity. Likewise His words: ﴿They fear people as they fear Allah or with greater fear﴾ [An-Nisa': 77], and His words: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [As-Saffat: 147], meaning: they were not fewer than that, rather they were in reality a hundred thousand, or more than that. This is a confirmation of what is reported, without doubt or hesitation, for such hesitation is impossible here. So too is this verse: ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾.

What we have said, that this one who drew near and came close, who became between him and Muhammad (ﷺ), is only Gabriel (peace be upon him), is the statement of the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Dharr and Abu Hurayrah, as we will soon cite their hadiths, Allah willing. Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice." [[Sahih Muslim, no. 176.]] He made this one of the two occasions. And there came in the hadith of Shurayk ibn Abi Namir, from Anas, in the hadith of the Night Journey: "Then the Compeller, the Lord of Might, drew near and descended." For this reason many people have spoken about the text (matn) of this narration, and they mentioned things in it that are strange. If it is authentic, then it is to be understood as referring to another time and another event, not as an explanation of this verse, for this was when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on the earth, not on the night of the Isra'. For this reason He said after it: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [An-Najm: 13–14]. So that is the night of the Isra', and the first was on the earth.

Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi al-Shawarib narrated to us, 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad narrated to us, Sulayman al-Shaybani narrated to us, Zirr ibn Hubaysh narrated to us, who said: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said concerning this verse, ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw Gabriel, he had six hundred wings." [[Tafsir al-Tabari (27/27).]]

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 53, verse 5–18 (part 2 of 3):

Ibn Wahb said: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from Abu al-Aswad, from 'Urwah, from 'Aishah, who said: The beginning of the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was that he saw Jibril in his dream at Ajyad. Then he went out to relieve himself, and Jibril called out to him: "O Muhammad, O Muhammad!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked to his right and to his left, and he saw nothing — three times. Then he raised his gaze, and behold, he was sitting with one leg over the other on the horizon of the sky. He said: "O Muhammad, Jibril, Jibril!" — calming him. The Prophet (ﷺ) fled until he entered among the people. He looked, but saw nothing. Then he came out from among the people, looked again, and saw him. He entered among the people, but saw nothing. Then he came out and looked, and saw him. That is the statement of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿By the star when it sets. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾, meaning Jibril drew near to Muhammad, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾. They say: "al-qab" is half a finger's length. Some of them said: it was the span of two cubits between them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the report of Ibn Wahb. And in the hadith of al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from Jabir, there is a witness to this.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Talq ibn Ghannam, from Za'idah, from al-Shaybani, who said: I asked Zirr about the statement: ﴿Then he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. He said: 'Abdullah told us that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bazi' al-Baghdadi narrated to me, Ishaq ibn Mansur narrated to us, Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, from 'Abdullah regarding: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril in two garments of green silk (rafraf), which filled what was between the heaven and the earth.

Based on what we have mentioned, His statement ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ means: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad, what he revealed. Or: Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad what He revealed through Jibril. Both meanings are correct. It has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His statement ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ that he said: He revealed to him: "Did We not find you an orphan?" ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharh: 4].

Others said: Allah revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it.

* *

As for His statement ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw. Will you then dispute with him over what he saw?﴾, Muslim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from Ziyad ibn Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ and ﴿He saw him in another descent﴾, he said: He saw him with his heart twice.

Similarly, Simak narrated it from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it. Likewise Abu Salih, al-Suddi and others said: He saw him with his heart twice [or once]. It has been opposed by Ibn Mas'ud and others. In one report from him (Ibn 'Abbas) he stated the seeing without qualification, and it is to be understood as restricted to the heart. As for whoever narrated from him that it was with the eye, he is unusual, for nothing authentic has come on this from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The statement of al-Baghawi in his tafsir: "A group went to the view that he saw Him with his own eye, and this is the view of Anas, al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah" — it is open to scrutiny, and Allah knows best.

Al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Nabhan ibn Safwan narrated to us, Yahya ibn Kathir al-'Anbari narrated to us, from Salm ibn Ja'far, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Muhammad saw his Lord. I said: Does not Allah say: ﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives all vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103]? He said: Woe to you! That is when He manifests Himself with His light which is His light; and he saw his Lord twice.

Then he said: Hasan gharib.

He also said: Ibn Abi 'Umar narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi who said: Ibn 'Abbas met Ka'b at 'Arafah, and asked him about something, and he exclaimed "Allahu akbar" until the mountains echoed back to him. Ibn 'Abbas said: We are the Banu Hashim. Ka'b said: Allah divided His seeing and His speech between Muhammad and Musa: Musa spoke with Him twice, and Muhammad saw Him twice. Masruq said: I entered upon 'Aishah and said: Did Muhammad see his Lord? She said: You have said something at which my hair stood on end. I said: Gently, then I recited: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾.

She said: Where are you being taken? It was only Jibril. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord, or that he concealed something of what he was commanded, or that he knows the five things which Allah, the Exalted, mentioned: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman: 34] — he has indeed uttered a great slander. Rather, he saw Jibril in his form only twice: once at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Jiyad, and he had six hundred wings, having filled the horizon.

Al-Nasa'i said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Do you wonder that the garment belongs to Ibrahim, the speech to Musa, and the seeing to Muhammad, peace be upon them?!

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "There is light; how could I see Him?" In another narration: "I saw a light."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Abu Khalid narrated to us, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart twice." Then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Ibn Humayd, from Mihran, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I did not see Him with my eye, but I saw Him with my heart twice," then he recited: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari narrated to us, 'Abbad ibn Mansur informed me who said: I asked 'Ikrimah: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. 'Ikrimah said: Do you want me to tell you that he has seen Him? I said: Yes. He said: He has seen Him, and then he has seen Him. He said: I asked al-Hasan about it, and he said: He saw His majesty, His greatness, and His robe.

And my father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Mujahid narrated to us, Abu 'Amir al-'Aqadi narrated to us, Abu Khaldah informed us, from Abu al-'Aliyah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and I saw behind the river a veil, and I saw behind the veil a light, I did not see other than that." [Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it as in al-Durr al-Manthur, and it is mursal.]

That is very unusual. As for the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad:

Aswad ibn 'Amir narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord, Mighty and Majestic."

Its chain is according to the conditions of the sahih, but it is an abridgement of the hadith of the dream, as Imam Ahmad also narrated:

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My Lord came to me last night in the best of forms — I think he meant in sleep — and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know over what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?'" He said: "I said: No. So He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coldness between my breasts — or he said my chest — and I knew what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. Then He said: 'O Muhammad, do you know over what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?'" He said: "I said: Yes, they dispute over the expiations and the degrees." He said: "And what are the expiations and the degrees?" He said: "I said: Remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, and completing ablution in hardship. Whoever does this lives in goodness, dies in goodness, and is free from his sins like the day his mother bore him. And He said: 'Say, O Muhammad, when you pray: O Allah, I ask You for good deeds and to abandon evil deeds, and love for the poor. And if You intend a trial for Your servants, take me to You without being tried.'" He said: "And the degrees are giving food, spreading the greeting of peace, and praying at night while people sleep."

It has already been mentioned at the end of Surah Sad, from Mu'adh, something similar. Ibn Jarir narrated it by another route from Ibn 'Abbas, and in it there is a different context and a strange addition, so he said:

Ahmad ibn 'Isa al-Tamimi narrated to me, Sulayman ibn 'Umar ibn Sayyar narrated to me, my father narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Zarbi, from Umar ibn Sulayman, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord in the best of forms, and He said to me: 'O Muhammad, do you know over what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?' I said: 'No, my Lord.' So He placed His hand between my shoulders, and I found its coldness between my breasts, and I knew what is in the heavens and the earth. I said: 'O my Lord, over the degrees and the expiations, and transferring the feet to the congregations, and waiting for prayer after prayer.' I said: 'O my Lord, You took Ibrahim as a friend and You spoke to Musa directly, and You did such and such.' He said: 'Did I not expand your breast? Did I not remove from you your burden? Did I not do for you? Did I not do?'" He said: "Then He conveyed to me things which I was not permitted to tell you." He said: "That is His statement in His Book: ﴿Then he drew near and descended. And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed. The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾; so He placed the light of my sight in my heart, and I looked at Him with my heart." Its chain is weak.

Al-Hafiz Ibn 'Asakir mentioned with his chain to Habbar ibn al-Aswad, may Allah be pleased with him, that 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, when he went out on a trade journey to Syria, said to the people of Makkah: "Know that I disbelieve in the One who drew near and descended." The statement reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Allah has set upon him one of His dogs." Habbar said: I was with them, and we alighted in a land abounding in lions. He said: I saw the lion come and begin to sniff the heads of the people one by one, until it reached 'Utbah and seized his head from among them.

Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned in the Sirah that this was in the land of al-Zarqa', and it was said: in al-Sarah; and that he feared that night, and they placed him among them and slept around him; the lion came and began to roar, then it stepped over them to him and crushed his head — may Allah curse him.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge﴾. This was the second time the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril in his true form in which God created him, and it was on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). We have already presented the hadiths about the Isra', with their chains and wordings, at the beginning of the chapter "Subhan" (Surah al-Isra'), so there is no need to repeat them here. It has been mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, affirmed that the Prophet saw his Lord on the night of the Isra', and he cited this verse as evidence. A group of the early and later scholars followed him, while groups of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, the Successors and others disagreed with him.

Imam Ahmad said: Hasan ibn Musa narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud concerning this verse, ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril, and he had six hundred wings, and from his feathers were scattered the tahawil (pearls and rubies)." [[Musnad (1/460).]] This is a good and strong chain (isnad: the chain of narrators).

Ahmad also said: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, Sharik narrated to us, from Jami' ibn Abi Rashid, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril in his form, and he had six hundred wings, each wing of which had blocked the horizon. From his wing there would fall tahawil, pearls and rubies, which only God knows. [[I did not find it in the Musnad, but al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned it in Atraf al-Musnad (4/158).]] Its chain is also good.

Ahmad also said: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Husayn narrated to me, 'Asim ibn Bahdalah narrated to me, who said: I heard Shaqiq ibn Salamah saying: I heard Ibn Mas'ud saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he had six hundred wings." I asked 'Asim about the wings, but he refused to tell me. Then one of his companions informed me that the wing is what lies between the east and the west. [[Musnad (1/407).]] This is also a good chain.

Ahmad said: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Husayn narrated to us, 'Asim ibn Bahdalah narrated to me, [[In A: "Husayn."]] Shaqiq narrated to me, [[In M: "Shaqiq ibn Salamah."]] who said: [[In M, A: "He said."]] I heard Ibn Mas'ud saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me wearing a green garment on which there were pearls." [[Musnad (1/407).]] Its chain is also good.

Imam Ahmad said: Yahya narrated to me, from Isma'il, Amir narrated to us, who said: Masruq came to 'A'ishah and said: O Mother of the Believers, did Muhammad (ﷺ) see his Lord, Mighty and Majestic? She said: Glory be to God! My hair stood on end at what you have said. Where are you from three things? Whoever tells you any of them has lied. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord has lied. Then she recited: ﴿No vision perceives Him, but He perceives all vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103], and ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. Whoever tells you that he knows what will happen tomorrow has lied. Then she recited: ﴿Indeed, God has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs﴾ [Luqman: 34] to the end of the verse. Whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed something has lied. Then she recited: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. Rather, he saw Jibril in his form twice. [[Musnad (6/49).]]

Ahmad also said: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, who said: I was with 'A'ishah and I said: Does not God say: ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir: 23], and ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾? She said: I am the first of this Ummah to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "That was only Jibril. I have not seen him in his form in which he was created except twice: I saw him descending from the sky to the earth, filling the vastness of his creation between the sky and the earth."

Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in their Sahihs, through the hadith of al-Sha'bi with this chain. [[Musnad (6/241), Sahih al-Bukhari no. (4855), and Sahih Muslim no. (177), in similar wording.]]

The narration of Abu Dharr: Imam Ahmad said: 'Affan narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, Qatadah narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, who said: I said to Abu Dharr: If I had seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would have asked him. He said: What would you have asked him? He said: I would have asked him: Did he see his Lord, Mighty and Majestic? He said: I did ask him, and he said: "I saw Him as light; how could I see Him?" [[Musnad (5/147).]]

This is what occurs in the narration of Imam Ahmad. Muslim also recorded it through two routes with two wordings. He said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, from Qatadah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Did you see your Lord? He said: "Light; how could I see Him?"

And he said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, my father narrated to us, from Qatadah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, who said: I said to Abu Dharr: If I had seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would have asked him. He said: About what would you have asked him? I said: I would have asked him: Did you see your Lord? Abu Dharr said: I did ask, and he said: "I saw light." [[Sahih Muslim no. (178).]]

Al-Khallal in his book "al-'Ilal" related that Imam Ahmad was asked about this hadith and said: I have always disapproved of it, and I do not know its meaning. [[The objection has no basis in the text, for it has supporting narrations, and it is evidence for the negation of seeing God in this world.]]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, 'Amr ibn 'Awn al-Wasiti narrated to us, Hushaym informed us, from Mansur, from al-Hakam, from Ibrahim, from his father, from Abu Dharr, who said: He saw Him with his heart, and did not see Him with his eye.

Ibn Khuzaymah tried to claim that there is a break in the chain between 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq and Abu Dharr. As for Ibn al-Jawzi, he interpreted it to mean that Abu Dharr perhaps asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before the Isra', and he answered him with what he answered; and if he had asked him after the Isra', he would have answered with affirmation. But this is very weak, for 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, may God be pleased with her, asked about it after the Isra', and it was not affirmed for her. Whoever says that he addressed her according to the level of her understanding, or tried to show her to be mistaken in what she held, such as Ibn Khuzaymah in his book "al-Tawhid" [[al-Tawhid of Ibn Khuzaymah (pp. 205, 206) (p. 225).]], then he himself is the one in error. And God knows best.

Al-Nasa'i said: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Hisham narrated to us, from Mansur, from al-Hakam, from Yazid ibn Shurayk, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, saw his Lord with his heart, and did not see Him with his eyes. [[al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra no. (11536).]]

It is established in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, from 'Ali ibn Mushir, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that he said concerning the verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾: He saw Jibril, peace be upon him. [[In A: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril."]] [[Sahih Muslim no. (175).]]

Mujahid said concerning the verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾: He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Jibril in his form twice. Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said the same.

* *

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾: It has already been mentioned in the hadiths of the Isra' that the angels covered it like crows, and the light of the Lord covered it, and colours covered it, which I do not know what they are.

Imam Ahmad said: Malik ibn Mighwal narrated to us, al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi narrated to us, from Talhah, from Murrah, from 'Abd Allah, that is Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, which is in the seventh heaven, to which whatever ascends from the earth ends, and it is taken from there; and to which whatever descends from above it ends, and it is taken from there. ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾. He said: It was a carpet of gold. He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever of his Ummah does not associate anything with God will be forgiven the grave sins. Muslim alone narrated it. [[Musnad (1/422) and Sahih Muslim no. (173).]]

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or another (Abu Ja'far was in doubt), who said: When the Messenger of God was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree, and it was said to him: This is the Lote-tree. [He said:] And the light of the Creator covered it, and the angels covered it like crows when they alight on a tree. He said: Then He spoke to him at that moment, and said to him: Ask.

Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid: ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾: He said: The branches of the Lote-tree were pearls, rubies and emeralds, and Muhammad saw it, and saw his Lord with his heart.

Ibn Zayd said: It was said: O Messenger of God, what did you see covering that Lote-tree? He said: "I saw a carpet of gold covering it, and I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying God, Mighty and Majestic." [[This is one of the mursal reports (lacking a Companion in the chain) of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who is weak.]]

* *

His saying: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It did not turn right or left. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: it did not go beyond what he was commanded.

This is a great attribute of steadfastness and obedience, for he did only what he was commanded, and he did not ask for more than he was given. How excellent is what the poet (al-Nazim) said:

He saw the Garden of Refuge and what lies above it, and had another seen what he saw, he would have been bewildered.

* *

His saying: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, like His saying: ﴿That We may show you of Our signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23], meaning: which indicate Our power and Our greatness. By these two verses, those among the People of the Sunnah who hold that the seeing (of God) did not occur that night have derived evidence; for He said: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, and if he had seen his Lord, he would have reported that and said so to the people. This has already been established in Surat al-Isra'. Imam Ahmad said:

Abu al-Nadr narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Talhah narrated to us, from al-Walid ibn Qays, from Ishaq ibn Abi al-Kahtalah. Muhammad said: I think it is from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: Muhammad did not see Jibril in his form except twice. As for one time, he asked him to show him himself in his form, and he showed him his form, and it filled the horizon. As for the other, he ascended with him when he ascended. And His saying: ﴿while he was at the highest horizon. Then he approached and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. And He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. He said: When Jibril perceived his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, he returned to his form and prostrated. So His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge, when there covered the Lote-tree that which covered. His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress. He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾: he said: [it refers to] the creation of Jibril, peace be upon him.

This is how Imam Ahmad narrated it, and it is strange (gharib). [[Musnad (1/407).]]

Ibn Kathir's commentary on Surah al-Najm (53), verses 5–18 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, exalted is He, says, informing about His servant and messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), that the one who taught him, the one who brought it to mankind, is ﴿mighty in power﴾. This is Gabriel (peace be upon him), as He said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, obeyed and trustworthy﴾ [At-Takwir: 19–21].

Here He says ﴿dhu mirrah﴾, meaning possessor of strength. This was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Abbas said: possessor of a fine appearance.

Qatadah said: possessor of a tall and handsome form.

There is no contradiction between the two statements, for he (peace be upon him) had a fine appearance and great strength. In the authentic hadith narrated through Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Amr, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity is not lawful for the rich, nor for one who possesses mirrah and is sound [of body]." [[The hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr is narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan, no. 1634, and by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan, no. 652, from Rayhan ibn Yazid, from him. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is narrated by al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (5/99) and Ibn Majah in his Sunan, no. 1839, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from him.]]

* *

His words ﴿Then he stood﴾ refer to Gabriel (peace be upon him). This was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

﴿while he was at the higher horizon﴾ refers to Gabriel, who stood at the higher horizon. This was said by 'Ikrimah and others. 'Ikrimah said: The higher horizon is the one from which the dawn comes. Mujahid said: it is the place where the sun rises. Qatadah said: it is the one from which the daytime comes. Ibn Zayd and others said likewise.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Zur'ah narrated to us, Musarrif ibn 'Amr al-Yami Abu al-Qasim narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Talhah ibn Musarrif narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from al-Walid (that is, Ibn Qays), from Ishaq ibn Abi al-Kahtalah, I think he mentioned it from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not see Gabriel in his [true] form except twice. The first time, he asked him to show himself in his form, and he filled the horizon. The second time, he was with him when he ascended, and that is His words: ﴿while he was at the higher horizon﴾.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) has made a statement here that I have not seen from anyone else, nor has he attributed it to anyone. Its essence is that he took the meaning to be: ﴿Then he stood﴾, that is, this mighty one of power, possessor of strength, together with Muhammad (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon both of them), ﴿while he was at the higher horizon﴾, that is, both of them stood together at the horizon, and that was on the night of the Isra'. Thus he said, and no one agreed with him in this. Then he proceeded to justify what he said from the standpoint of Arabic grammar (al-'Arabiyyah), and said: This is like His words: ﴿When we are dust and our fathers [are brought forth]?﴾ [An-Naml: 67], where he joined "al-aba'" (the fathers) to the pronoun in "kunna" (we were) without making "nahnu" (we) explicit. Likewise His words: ﴿Then he stood, while he﴾. He said: al-Farra' mentioned from some of the Arabs that he recited:

Have you not seen that the nab' tree hardens its wood,
while the brittle castor plant does not stand alike?

[The line is in Tafsir al-Tabari (27/25) and is by Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah.]

What he said from the standpoint of Arabic grammar is sound, but the meaning does not support it, for this vision of Gabriel was not on the night of the Isra'; rather it was before that, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on the earth. Gabriel descended to him and drew near to him, while he was in the form in which Allah created him, having six hundred wings. Then he saw him another time, a descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), that is, on the night of the Isra'. This first vision was in the early days of the prophethood, after Gabriel (peace be upon him) had come to him for the first time, when Allah revealed to him the opening verses of "Iqra'" (Surah al-'Alaq). Then the revelation paused for a period, during which the Prophet (ﷺ) went out many times, intending to throw himself from the mountain peaks. Whenever he was about to do that, Gabriel would call out to him from the air: "O Muhammad, you are truly the Messenger of Allah, and I am Gabriel." Thereby his heart would be calmed and his eye comforted. Whenever the matter lasted long for him, he would return to it again, until Gabriel appeared to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in al-Abtah, in his form in which Allah created him, having six hundred wings, which filled the horizon with the greatness of his body. He drew near to him and revealed to him from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, what He commanded him. At that moment he recognized the greatness of the angel who had brought him the message, the nobility of his rank, and the high station he held with his Creator who had sent him.

As for the hadith which the memorizer (al-Hafiz) Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated in his Musnad, where he said:

Salamah ibn Shabib narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated to us, al-Harith ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us, from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While I was sitting, Gabriel (peace be upon him) came, and struck between my shoulders. I rose toward a tree in which there were two nests of birds, and he sat in one of them and I sat in the other. It rose and ascended until it filled the two horizons, while I was turning my gaze. Had I wished to touch the sky, I would have touched it. Gabriel turned to me as if he were a rug laid down, and I recognized the excellence of his knowledge of Allah over me. A door of the doors of heaven was opened for me, and I saw the Greatest Light, and beneath the Veil was a fluttering of pearls and rubies. And what Allah willed to reveal was revealed to me."

Then al-Bazzar said: No one narrates it except al-Harith ibn 'Ubayd, and he was a well-known man from the people of Basra. [[Musnad al-Bazzar, no. 58.]]

I say: This al-Harith ibn 'Ubayd is Abu Qudamah al-Iyadi. Muslim included him in his Sahih, but Ibn Ma'in weakened him and said: he is not anything. Imam Ahmad said: his hadith is inconsistent (mudtarib). Abu Hatim al-Razi said: his hadith is written down but is not used as evidence. Ibn Hibban said: his errors are many, so it is not permissible to use him as evidence when he is alone in a narration. This hadith is among his strange narrations, for it contains strangeness, unusual wording, and a strange context. Perhaps it was a dream, and Allah knows best.

Imam Ahmad said: Hajjaj narrated to us, Shurayk narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Gabriel in his form, and he had six hundred wings, each wing of which filled the horizon. From his wings there fell pearls, rubies and colored decorations, which only Allah knows. Ahmad alone narrated it. [[Al-Musnad (1/395).]]

Ahmad also said: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from Idris ibn Munabbih, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) asked Gabriel to show himself to him in his form. He said: "Ask your Lord." So he asked his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and a dark mass appeared to him from the east, which rose and spread out. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw it, he fainted. Gabriel came to him, supported him, and wiped the foam from his mouth.

Ahmad alone narrated it. [[Al-Musnad (1/322).]] Ibn 'Asakir also narrated it in the biography of 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, through the route of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from Habbar ibn al-Aswad, who said: Abu Lahab and his son 'Utbah had prepared to go to Syria, and I prepared with them. His son 'Utbah said: "By Allah, I will go to Muhammad and I will harm him concerning his Lord, Glorified is He." So he went until he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, he (Allah) disbelieves in the One who drew near and came down, so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, send against him one of Your dogs." Then he left him and returned to his father. His father said: "My son, what did you say to him?" He told him what he had said to him. He said: "What did he say to you?" He said: "He said: 'O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs.'" He said: "My son, by Allah, I do not feel safe from his supplication against you." So we travelled until we stopped at al-Shurah, which was a lion-infested place, and we went down to the hermitage of a monk. The monk said: "O company of the Arabs, what brought you to this land? Lions roam in it as sheep roam." Abu Lahab said to us: "You know my old age and my right, and this man has made a supplication against my son, which, by Allah, I do not feel safe from. So gather your goods at this hermitage, spread them out for my son upon it, then spread out around it." We did so, and the lion came and smelled our faces. When it did not find what it wanted, it crouched, then leapt, and behold, it was on top of the goods. It smelled his face, then struck him a blow that crushed his head. Abu Lahab said: "I knew that he would not escape the supplication of Muhammad." [[I have not found the biography of 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab in the manuscript of Tarikh Dimashq, nor in its abridgment by Ibn Manzur.]]

* *

His words ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾ mean: Gabriel drew near to Muhammad when he descended to him on the earth, until there was between him and Muhammad (ﷺ) the distance of two bow-lengths, that is, the measure of the two when they are stretched. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

It has also been said that what is meant is the distance between the string of the bow and its belly (the wooden body).

* *

His words ﴿or nearer﴾: it has already been mentioned that this expression is used in the language to affirm what is being reported and to negate anything beyond it, as in His words: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74], meaning: they are not softer than stones, rather they are like them or exceed them in hardness and severity. Likewise His words: ﴿They fear people as they fear Allah or with greater fear﴾ [An-Nisa': 77], and His words: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [As-Saffat: 147], meaning: they were not fewer than that, rather they were in reality a hundred thousand, or more than that. This is a confirmation of what is reported, without doubt or hesitation, for such hesitation is impossible here. So too is this verse: ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾.

What we have said, that this one who drew near and came close, who became between him and Muhammad (ﷺ), is only Gabriel (peace be upon him), is the statement of the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Dharr and Abu Hurayrah, as we will soon cite their hadiths, Allah willing. Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice." [[Sahih Muslim, no. 176.]] He made this one of the two occasions. And there came in the hadith of Shurayk ibn Abi Namir, from Anas, in the hadith of the Night Journey: "Then the Compeller, the Lord of Might, drew near and descended." For this reason many people have spoken about the text (matn) of this narration, and they mentioned things in it that are strange. If it is authentic, then it is to be understood as referring to another time and another event, not as an explanation of this verse, for this was when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on the earth, not on the night of the Isra'. For this reason He said after it: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [An-Najm: 13–14]. So that is the night of the Isra', and the first was on the earth.

Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi al-Shawarib narrated to us, 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad narrated to us, Sulayman al-Shaybani narrated to us, Zirr ibn Hubaysh narrated to us, who said: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said concerning this verse, ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw Gabriel, he had six hundred wings." [[Tafsir al-Tabari (27/27).]]

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 53, verse 5–18 (part 2 of 3):

Ibn Wahb said: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from Abu al-Aswad, from 'Urwah, from 'Aishah, who said: The beginning of the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was that he saw Jibril in his dream at Ajyad. Then he went out to relieve himself, and Jibril called out to him: "O Muhammad, O Muhammad!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked to his right and to his left, and he saw nothing — three times. Then he raised his gaze, and behold, he was sitting with one leg over the other on the horizon of the sky. He said: "O Muhammad, Jibril, Jibril!" — calming him. The Prophet (ﷺ) fled until he entered among the people. He looked, but saw nothing. Then he came out from among the people, looked again, and saw him. He entered among the people, but saw nothing. Then he came out and looked, and saw him. That is the statement of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿By the star when it sets. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾, meaning Jibril drew near to Muhammad, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾. They say: "al-qab" is half a finger's length. Some of them said: it was the span of two cubits between them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the report of Ibn Wahb. And in the hadith of al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from Jabir, there is a witness to this.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Talq ibn Ghannam, from Za'idah, from al-Shaybani, who said: I asked Zirr about the statement: ﴿Then he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. He said: 'Abdullah told us that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bazi' al-Baghdadi narrated to me, Ishaq ibn Mansur narrated to us, Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, from 'Abdullah regarding: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril in two garments of green silk (rafraf), which filled what was between the heaven and the earth.

Based on what we have mentioned, His statement ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ means: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad, what he revealed. Or: Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad what He revealed through Jibril. Both meanings are correct. It has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His statement ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ that he said: He revealed to him: "Did We not find you an orphan?" ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharh: 4].

Others said: Allah revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it.

* *

As for His statement ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw. Will you then dispute with him over what he saw?﴾, Muslim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from Ziyad ibn Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ and ﴿He saw him in another descent﴾, he said: He saw him with his heart twice.

Similarly, Simak narrated it from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it. Likewise Abu Salih, al-Suddi and others said: He saw him with his heart twice [or once]. It has been opposed by Ibn Mas'ud and others. In one report from him (Ibn 'Abbas) he stated the seeing without qualification, and it is to be understood as restricted to the heart. As for whoever narrated from him that it was with the eye, he is unusual, for nothing authentic has come on this from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The statement of al-Baghawi in his tafsir: "A group went to the view that he saw Him with his own eye, and this is the view of Anas, al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah" — it is open to scrutiny, and Allah knows best.

Al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Nabhan ibn Safwan narrated to us, Yahya ibn Kathir al-'Anbari narrated to us, from Salm ibn Ja'far, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Muhammad saw his Lord. I said: Does not Allah say: ﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives all vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103]? He said: Woe to you! That is when He manifests Himself with His light which is His light; and he saw his Lord twice.

Then he said: Hasan gharib.

He also said: Ibn Abi 'Umar narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi who said: Ibn 'Abbas met Ka'b at 'Arafah, and asked him about something, and he exclaimed "Allahu akbar" until the mountains echoed back to him. Ibn 'Abbas said: We are the Banu Hashim. Ka'b said: Allah divided His seeing and His speech between Muhammad and Musa: Musa spoke with Him twice, and Muhammad saw Him twice. Masruq said: I entered upon 'Aishah and said: Did Muhammad see his Lord? She said: You have said something at which my hair stood on end. I said: Gently, then I recited: ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾.

She said: Where are you being taken? It was only Jibril. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord, or that he concealed something of what he was commanded, or that he knows the five things which Allah, the Exalted, mentioned: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman: 34] — he has indeed uttered a great slander. Rather, he saw Jibril in his form only twice: once at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Jiyad, and he had six hundred wings, having filled the horizon.

Al-Nasa'i said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Do you wonder that the garment belongs to Ibrahim, the speech to Musa, and the seeing to Muhammad, peace be upon them?!

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "There is light; how could I see Him?" In another narration: "I saw a light."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Abu Khalid narrated to us, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart twice." Then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Ibn Humayd, from Mihran, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I did not see Him with my eye, but I saw Him with my heart twice," then he recited: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari narrated to us, 'Abbad ibn Mansur informed me who said: I asked 'Ikrimah: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. 'Ikrimah said: Do you want me to tell you that he has seen Him? I said: Yes. He said: He has seen Him, and then he has seen Him. He said: I asked al-Hasan about it, and he said: He saw His majesty, His greatness, and His robe.

And my father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Mujahid narrated to us, Abu 'Amir al-'Aqadi narrated to us, Abu Khaldah informed us, from Abu al-'Aliyah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and I saw behind the river a veil, and I saw behind the veil a light, I did not see other than that." [Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it as in al-Durr al-Manthur, and it is mursal.]

That is very unusual. As for the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad:

Aswad ibn 'Amir narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord, Mighty and Majestic."

Its chain is according to the conditions of the sahih, but it is an abridgement of the hadith of the dream, as Imam Ahmad also narrated:
